title: Train/test splits and overfitting
learner_summary: A sophomore at Colorado School of Mines who has taken CSCI 128 and is comfortable writing Python. They have minimal data science experience: they have never trained a model and have never held out data to test one.

objectives.text: Explain why a model is evaluated on held-out test data that it never saw during training.
Recognize overfitting by comparing a model's training score with its test score.
Choose between a single train/test split, a validation set and cross-validation for a given situation.

facts.text: An overfit model has learned the training data too closely, including its noise and quirks, instead of the general pattern, so it does not carry over to new data.
The sign of overfitting is a large gap between the scores: the training score is very high while the test score is much lower.
An overfit model has a much higher training score than an underfit model, because an underfit model scores low on the training data too.

misconceptions.text: A high training accuracy means the model is good enough, no matter what its test score is.
misconceptions.correction: The training score only shows how well the model fits data it has already seen; the test score shows how it will do on new data, which is what the model is for. A high training score with a low test score is overfitting.

misconceptions.text: Underfitting and overfitting are the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: They are opposites: an underfit model is too simple and scores low on both training and test data, while an overfit model fits the training data too closely and scores high on training data but much lower on test data.

misconceptions.text: Overfitting lowers both the training accuracy and the test accuracy.
misconceptions.correction: Overfitting raises the training accuracy while the test accuracy falls; a model that does poorly on both is underfitting.

misconceptions.text: Measuring accuracy on the training data gives a fair score for the model.
misconceptions.correction: The model has already learned from the training data, so its score there is too optimistic; only data it has never seen shows how it will do on new data.

misconceptions.text: It is fine to look at the test score while choosing or tuning the model.
misconceptions.correction: Every choice made by looking at the test score fits the model a little to the test set, so it is no longer unseen and its score becomes too optimistic; choices should be made with a validation set, and the test set used once at the end.
